week.t: NASA: Swift expected to re-enter on Wednesday 4 Nov, 22 years after launch; risk to anyone 1 in 2,100
NASA: ESCAPADE’s twin probes to make powered Earth flybys on 7 and 9 Nov, then cruise to Mars
Hubble: 37 dwarf galaxies are missing most of their oxygen; supernova winds blamed
Science News Explores: Japan’s baseball-sized SORA-Q rover swims through Moon dust
ISRO: first orbit-raising burn on NVS-03, 2,174.8 s, perigee lifted from 170 km to 5,478 km
Landsat 8 imaged Pine Creek Gorge in full autumn colour on 25 Oct; NASA’s Image of the Day

tiles.cap: Swift, built for 2 years, watched the sky for 22. On Wednesday it falls out of it
tiles.nums: NASA’s estimate of the risk that a surviving piece harms anyone on Earth
tiles.p1: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday 4 November, almost 22 years after launch. As of Monday the US Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound (about 1,450 kg) spacecraft will come down at about 3:30 am US Eastern time, which is 4:30 pm in Singapore, with an uncertainty of 11 hours either way. NASA expects most of it to burn up, but some components are expected to survive.
tiles.p2: Why here: because Swift orbits at a low tilt, any surviving fragments can only land between 20.6° south and 20.6° north. Singapore, at about 1.3° north, sits inside that band.
deep: What Swift did

Swift launched in 2004 to catch gamma-ray bursts, the brightest explosions in the universe, and was designed for a two-year prime mission. It kept working for more than two decades of science operations.
The odds
NASA puts the risk of harm to anyone on Earth at approximately 1 in 2,100. That is the chance for the whole planet combined; for any one person it is a tiny fraction of that.
The band

Swift’s orbit has a low inclination, so NASA says re-entry locations of surviving fragments are limited to between 20.6 degrees south and 20.6 degrees north latitude. Everywhere outside that band is out of the question.
Watch the update
NASA and the Space Force say they will keep monitoring the re-entry and updating the prediction, so the Wednesday-afternoon estimate for Singapore could move by hours either way.
tiles.src: NASA Swift blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Alise Fisher, Goddard)

tiles.cap: Two fridge-sized probes skim Earth on Saturday evening, fire engines, and leave for Mars
tiles.nums: the length of each trans-Mars injection burn, adding more than 1,000 mph (about 1,600 km/h)
tiles.p1: NASA’s twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will each perform a manoeuvre no agency spacecraft has flown before, a powered flyby of Earth, one after the other. The first makes its closest approach and finishes its engine burn around 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 November, which is 6 pm in Singapore; the second follows around 6 am Eastern on Monday 9 November, 7 pm here. Each burn is made over southern Australia and raises the craft’s speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second (roughly 10.1 to 10.8 km/s).
tiles.p2: Why now: ESCAPADE launched in November 2025 when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun, so the pair looped around Earth–Sun Lagrange point 2 in a loiter orbit, waiting for the right moment to be thrown onward.
deep: How close

Closest approach is between 600 and 1,100 miles (roughly 970 to 1,770 km) above the surface. At the speed they leave, NASA says, the spacecraft could fly from Washington, DC, to San Francisco in less than 7 minutes, about Mach 30 to Mach 31.
Then the long cruise

After the flybys comes a 10-month cruise. Arrival at Mars is set for 7 and 9 September 2027, where the pair will be the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around the planet, measuring how the solar wind strips away the Martian atmosphere.
Bonus science on the way
While loitering, the spacecraft flew through a distant part of Earth’s magnetotail, the long magnetic wake the solar wind drags out behind our planet. NASA says those findings will be shared soon.
Can you see them
NASA says the spacecraft are faint and a telescope will most likely be needed; the coordinates come from JPL’s Horizons system. Each one is about the size of a standard refrigerator.
tiles.src: NASA ESCAPADE blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas, Goddard)
tiles.credit: Image: Advanced Space / Matt Bolliger, via NASA

tiles.cap: Hubble looked at 37 small galaxies and found most of their oxygen has gone missing
tiles.nums: nearby dwarf galaxies, each holding a few thousand to hundreds of millions of stars
tiles.p1: In a paper published on Monday in The Astrophysical Journal, researchers using the Hubble Space Telescope looked at 37 nearby dwarf galaxies and found that much of the oxygen they expected to see is missing. Oxygen is the most abundant element after hydrogen and helium, and it is made inside stars, so a galaxy full of stars should be keeping it.
tiles.p2: The suspect: galactic winds. Supernovae blow gas out of these small galaxies, and the winds turn out to be far better at removing oxygen from low-mass galaxies than current models predict.
deep: Why small galaxies lose

A dwarf galaxy has weak gravity, so when a star explodes, the hot gas it throws out can escape altogether instead of falling back. NASA says the findings show dwarf galaxies can hold on to only a small fraction of the oxygen their stars make.
The programme

The work is called GLOW, Galaxies Losing Oxygen via Winds, funded by NASA and the National Science Foundation. Kristen Wingfield McQuinn of Rutgers leads it, with Grace Telford of the University of Utah as a co-investigator.
More than Hubble

The team combined archival Hubble images with data from NASA’s retired Spitzer Space Telescope, the Very Large Array and the Australian Telescope Compact Array. A similar look at Milky Way-sized galaxies was done in 2014.
Next
McQuinn has an approved programme on the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to follow up, and Telford will use Hubble to look at massive stars.
tiles.src: NASA Hubble news, 2 Nov 2026 · The Astrophysical Journal, doi 10.3847/1538-4357/ae93a6
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA, ESA, Hubble Heritage / A. Aloisi (STScI, ESA)

tiles.cap: A 36-minute engine burn lifted India’s new navigation satellite from 170 km to 5,478 km
tiles.nums: the first Liquid Apogee Motor burn on NVS-03, completed on Saturday at 16:48 Indian time
tiles.p1: GSLV-F18 injected NVS-03 into a 170.3 km × 38,080 km orbit on 30 October at 23:51 IST, which was 2:21 am on Saturday in Singapore. The next afternoon ISRO fired the satellite’s LAM engine for 2,174.8 seconds, and the orbit became 5,477.6 km × 37,833.4 km. The satellite’s health is normal, and further burns in the coming days will place it in geostationary orbit at 111.75° east.
tiles.p2: Why the numbers matter: a transfer orbit is a lopsided ellipse. Each burn near the high point lifts the low point, so the orbit is rounded off step by step rather than in one go.
deep: What NVS-03 is

It is the third satellite in India’s next-generation navigation system, meant to continue the IRNSS series, which provides navigation services over the Indian land mass and a region extending 1,500 km around the country’s borders. It carries an indigenous atomic clock alongside procured ones and adds an L1 signal to the existing L5 and S-band signals.
The launcher

GSLV-F18 was the 20th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle, flown from the Second Launch Pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota. ISRO calls the destination a Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit.
Why 111.75° east

A geostationary satellite circles once a day, so from the ground it seems to hang over one longitude. ISRO’s target slot is 111.75° east, from which the satellite stays in view of India all day, every day.
Where it is now
After one burn the low point is already above 5,000 km while the high point barely moved, from 38,080 km to 37,833.4 km. Count how many burns ISRO reports before the orbit is round.
tiles.src: ISRO, Orbit manoeuvring of NVS-03 spacecraft, 31 Oct 2026 · ISRO GSLV-F18 mission page
tiles.credit: Photo: ISRO, GSLV-F18 on the pad

tiles.cap: A 460-metre-deep gash in Pennsylvania, photographed from orbit as the forest turns orange
tiles.nums: the length of Pine Creek Gorge, from Ansonia south to the West Branch Susquehanna
tiles.p1: The Operational Land Imager on Landsat 8 captured Pine Creek Gorge on 25 October 2026, amid the warm hues of fall foliage. The gorge, called Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon, reaches depths of about 1,500 feet (460 metres) and runs some 45 miles (72 km); it is deepest around Waterville. NASA Earth Observatory published it as its Image of the Day on Monday.
tiles.p2: Why the river runs the wrong way: Pine Creek once flowed to the north. Glaciers dammed the river and filled the valley with lakes; today it drains south to the Susquehanna.
deep: Two dates, one place

NASA paired the 25 October image with one from 9 October, so you can see the colour sweep across the plateau in just over two weeks. The full-size 25 October file is 47.9 megabytes; the 9 October one is 15.3.
From desert to landmark

Logging stripped the slopes so completely that by the early 20th century the area was known as the Pennsylvania Desert. The forest grew back, and in 1968 an area of 30,000 acres (12,000 hectares) was designated a National Natural Landmark.
Where

Pine Creek Gorge forms a deep scar in the Allegheny Plateau, in north-central Pennsylvania. NASA’s page pairs the satellite view with a ground photo taken from Colton Point State Park, on the gorge’s rim, in October 2009.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, Image of the Day, 2 Nov 2026 (story by Lindsey Doermann; image by Michala Garrison)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, Landsat 8

tiles.cap: A Moon rover the size of a baseball, designed with a toy company. It swims through dust
tiles.nums: how long SORA-Q crawled around its landing site after JAXA’s SLIM touched down on the Moon
tiles.p1: SORA-Q, from sora (space) and kyu (sphere), with a Q for quest and question, is about the starting size and shape of a baseball and weighs as much as a cup of water. It rode to the Moon on Japan’s SLIM lander, which reached the surface on 19 January 2024, and was dropped seconds before touchdown. It then crawled for more than 90 minutes and drove to about 5 metres from SLIM. Compare Perseverance and Curiosity, the size of small cars.
tiles.p2: Why a toy company: JAXA engineer Daichi Hirano wanted something small and cheap that might also reach cramped spaces, so his team worked with toy engineers at TOMY, the company that owns Transformers in Japan.
deep: The swimming trick

Smaller wheels get stuck more easily in powdery regolith, so SORA-Q’s wheels are offset and sweep up and down in circles. One wheel sweeping up while the other goes down makes it crawl; both in sync and it does a butterfly stroke through the dust.
Packaging

The design was published in Science Robotics on 10 June 2026 by Hirano and colleagues. Keenan Albee, a roboticist at the University of Southern California who was not involved, said the most impressive part to him was the packaging: a ball that unfolds into a rover.
Why small
NASA’s VIPER rover design was the size of a golf cart. Hirano, at JAXA in Sagamihara, says small rovers cost less and might also be able to reach cramped spaces that a big machine cannot.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 2 Nov 2026 (Kendra Redmond) · Science Robotics, Hirano et al., 10 June 2026

tiles.cap: Drop a magnet down a copper pipe and it falls in slow motion. Nothing is touching it
tiles.nums: of copper, aluminium or brass tube is enough; a pencil clatters straight through, the magnet dawdles
tiles.p1: The Exploratorium’s Eddy Currents snack needs a 60 cm to 1 m length of aluminium, copper or brass tubing (not iron) and a neodymium disc magnet at least 1.25 cm across and longer than it is wide. Drop the magnet through and notice that it takes noticeably more time to fall than a plastic pen or wooden pencil does. Try the same through a plastic PVC tube and the magic is gone.
tiles.p2: What is going on: the falling magnet’s changing field pushes the tube’s electrons round in circular, eddy-like currents. Those currents make their own magnetic field, which pushes back on the magnet, so it falls much more slowly.
deep: Feynman’s pendulum

In the Feynman Lectures a copper plate swings as a pendulum between the poles of an electromagnet. Switch the magnet on and the swing is suddenly arrested: the eddy currents exert a strong resistance to the motion, just like the viscous drag in honey. Cut slots in the plate and the braking is drastically reduced, because the currents can no longer flow in big loops.
Lenz’s rule

Feynman’s one-line version: the emf tries to oppose any flux change. The currents in the tube always flow the way that fights the magnet’s motion, which is why the tube only ever slows the magnet and never speeds it up.
Perfect conductor

Feynman adds that below 3.8 kelvin tin conducts perfectly, and if you put an electromagnet next to a sheet of perfect conductor, eddy currents appear in the sheet so that no magnetic flux enters at all.
A slower version

Two flat aluminium plates about 6 mm thick, spaced just wider than the magnet, give a remarkably slow rate of fall; allow at least a 15 cm drop. The same physics is why transformer cores are built from laminated sheets, and why eddy currents are used to damp the swing of mechanical balances.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Eddy Currents · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II, ch. 16

tiles.cap: A phone screen only its owner can read: two kinds of pixels, and the wide ones switch off
tiles.nums: peak brightness measured by Tom’s Guide, against 1,860 on last year’s S25 Ultra: dimmer, even with privacy off
tiles.p1: The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra made TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list as “a privacy-focused smartphone”. Its 6.9-inch display has two different kinds of pixels, narrow and wide; in privacy mode the wide pixels turn off, which limits what can be seen from the side, with no stick-on filter. Samsung lists it at 214 g, 7.9 mm thick, with a 5,000 mAh battery, a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip, a 200-megapixel main camera and an Armor Aluminum frame.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: Tom’s Guide measured 1,806 nits peak against 1,860 for last year’s S25 Ultra, dimmer across the board even with privacy off, and listed narrower viewing angles, a camera bump that makes the phone wobble when laid flat, and still no Qi2 magnets.
deep: The engineering

Samsung describes the feature as controlling the screen’s viewing angle to limit peripheral vision, and calls it the world’s first Privacy Display on mobile. TechRadar’s description: the panel has narrow and wide pixels, and in privacy mode the wide pixels turn off. It can be set for the whole screen or only for PINs, passwords and notification pop-ups, and per app.
What the lab found

Tom’s Guide measured 586 nits with Maximum Privacy on and 588 with it off, so the person holding the phone loses almost nothing. The whole panel, though, is dimmer than before: 1,209 nits in auto-brightness against 1,231 on the S25 Ultra, while Samsung rates it at up to 2,600 nits.
Complaints

By mid-March some owners were reporting blurry lettering, eye strain and headaches on Reddit; Tom’s Guide noted it was not clear how widespread the problem was, or whether it was the privacy feature or the panel itself. Samsung’s suggested fixes were dark mode, extra dim and Eye Comfort Shield.
The rest of the phone

TechRadar’s review calls it Samsung’s best Galaxy S phone yet but an iterative update, with no more titanium frame and no MagSafe-style magnets. Battery life in Tom’s Guide’s web test: 16 h 10 min, nearly two hours more than the S25 Ultra. Price $1,299.99.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 · Samsung spec page · Tom’s Guide review and lab tests, March 2026 · TechRadar review, 2 Mar 2026

tiles.cap: NTU built an AI that writes port-operations software in about an hour, for about S$12.70
tiles.nums: how close LACE’s algorithms came to the best result from any method tested, on four new maritime problems
tiles.p1: A new NTU system called LACE could cut the design of algorithms for complex scheduling, routing and resource-allocation problems from months to about an hour. Tested on four new maritime problems, its software scored 97 to 99 per cent against the best result obtained by any method tested, with runs taking about an hour and under US$10 (S$12.70) in computation fees per problem.
tiles.p2: Why it matters here: Singapore runs one of the busiest ports on Earth, and deciding which ship berths where, and when, is exactly the kind of problem this is built for.
deep: How it works

LACE stands for Large Language Model-driven Algorithm Construction via Complementary Evolution. LACE first breaks a problem into modular pieces, then uses a large language model to build and evolve a team of specialist rules whose strengths complement each other, keeping and refining the best portfolio.
Who built it

The work is led by Asst Prof Yan Ran and Research Fellow Dr Gong Huatian of NTU’s School of Civil and Environmental Engineering. The paper was published in Nature Machine Intelligence on 1 October 2026.
Versus Google

The team compared it with Google’s FunSearch, which, NTU says, failed completely to produce feasible algorithms or software for these problems. Dr Gong notes that traditional design of such software can take months and cost hundreds of thousands.
Test it yourself

Give a chatbot a small scheduling puzzle, three ships and two berths with different arrival times, and ask it for a rule rather than an answer. Then make a fourth ship arrive early and see whether the rule still holds.
tiles.src: NTU Singapore Research Hub, 8 Oct 2026 · Nature Machine Intelligence, doi 10.1038/s42256-026-01307-8

tiles.cap: Stare at the black dot: the blue blur beside it quietly vanishes. Move your eyes: back
tiles.nums: the size of the paper dot in the Exploratorium’s version, seen through waxed paper until its edges blur
tiles.p1: Look at the small black dot on this tile and keep your eyes and head perfectly still. The fuzzy blue patch next to it fades until it blends into the pink, and it comes back the moment you move your eyes. The Exploratorium’s Fading Dot snack does it with a 1-inch (2.5 cm) blue paper dot on pink paper under a sheet of waxed paper, lifted until the blue is very faint.
tiles.p2: What is going on: your eyes make tiny jittering movements all the time, and each movement sends new information to the brain. A blurred edge changes so gradually that the jitter brings nothing new, so the brain stops reporting it. If the dot had a distinct border your eyes would immediately detect the change.
deep: Why the rest stays sharp
Everything else on the page keeps its crisp edges, so every micro-movement refreshes it. Only the thing with no edge can slip away.
Fog

The Exploratorium notes a 2003 paper in the Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Neural Networks reporting that moving cars seem to slow down in foggy conditions: low contrast reduces perceived speed.
Make your own

Cut a 2.5 cm blue dot, put it in the centre of a pink sheet, lay waxed paper on top and lift the waxed paper toward your face until the blue is just a faint smudge. Then fix your gaze beside it. Try other colour pairs.
Related

This is a cousin of the afterimage: both come from your visual system adapting to anything that does not change. The difference is that here nothing is burned in; the signal simply stops being reported.

tiles.cap: Mars and Jupiter pass 1.2° apart on 15–16 November, and three supermoons start on the 24th
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors at best, before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set
tiles.p1: NASA’s What’s Up for November 2026, presented by Raquel Villanueva of JPL: the Southern Taurids peak around 5 November with occasional bright fireballs; the Northern Taurids around the 12th at about five meteors an hour; Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish; and the Leonids run before dawn on 17–18 November, up to around 15 an hour under ideal skies.
tiles.p2: Why here: Singapore sits almost on the equator, so Mars and Jupiter rise steeply in the east before dawn, and a full Moon on 24 November, the first of three supermoons in a row, climbs high overhead.
deep: Moon phases

Third quarter 1 November, new Moon on the 8th, first quarter on the 17th, full supermoon on the 24th, third quarter again on the 30th. The new Moon week, 5–12 November, is the dark window for the Taurids.
1.2 degrees

A common rule of thumb: your little finger at arm’s length covers about one degree of sky. Mars and Jupiter will sit about a finger apart, close enough to share a view in binoculars but easy to tell apart by colour.
A light-day away
On 17 November NASA marks Voyager 1 becoming the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: a radio message sent that day takes a full 24 hours to reach it.
Seeing meteors

NASA’s advice for the Leonids: find a dark location and give your eyes about half an hour to adjust. In Singapore that means a dark park or beach with an open eastern sky in the hours before dawn, once the Moon has set.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, 48% more problems right. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: they had the answers without doing the thinking, so nothing stuck.
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, opposite result.
What the researchers concluded
The problem was not AI. It was asking for the answer instead of asking for help. The researchers call the result a cautionary tale.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later. This includes the maths set-up your dad built with Claude.

tiles.cap: Your name can fly to Titan on NASA’s Dragonfly. The passenger list closes 15 January
tiles.nums: the year Dragonfly arrives at Saturn’s moon Titan, after a launch scheduled for 2028
tiles.p1: NASA is inviting the public to send their names aboard Dragonfly, a rotorcraft, and be part of the first science mission to fly and explore the surface of another world. The passenger list is open until 11:59 pm US Eastern time on 15 January 2027. Scheduled to launch in 2028, Dragonfly will travel to Titan, a world with a thick atmosphere, rivers and lakes of liquid methane, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material.
tiles.p2: Why it matters to you: NASA’s sign-up is a web form called “Send Your Name to Titan”, and it issues a personalised digital boarding pass. The deadline in Singapore time is 12:59 pm on Saturday 16 January.
deep: A rotorcraft on another moon

After arriving in 2034, Dragonfly will fly to different locations on the moon, exploring Titan’s diverse environments and searching for clues about prebiotic chemistry, the chemistry that came before biology, to help scientists better understand the ingredients and conditions for life.
Flying, not driving

NASA describes Titan as a remarkable world with a thick atmosphere, rivers and lakes of liquid methane, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material. Dragonfly will fly to different locations on the moon; NASA calls it the first science mission to fly and explore the surface of another world.
Who runs it

Dragonfly is the fourth mission in NASA’s New Frontiers Program, managed by NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, for the agency’s Science Mission Directorate. Elizabeth Turtle of APL, the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory, is the principal investigator.
The arithmetic of waiting
Sign up by January 2027, launch in 2028, arrive in 2034: your name spends about six years in flight. Add eight to your age now, and that is how old you will be when it lands.

tiles.cap: Flatten a straw, snip two lips, blow: a buzzing oboe. Snip it shorter and the note climbs
tiles.nums: the speed of every sound wave in air, high note or low, according to the Exploratorium
tiles.p1: Sound is a branch of mechanics, Feynman says, and so it is to be understood in terms of Newton’s laws: move something in the air and the air is compressed, a change of pressure is produced which pushes on additional air, and the disturbance travels. The Exploratorium’s Straw Oboe lets you hear the whole chain. Flatten one end of a plastic straw between your teeth, cut equal pieces from each side of the flattened end so the straw has two “lips”, seal your lips around it and blow, adjusting how hard you bite and blow until the straw sings.
tiles.p2: Test it: snip the straw shorter and shorter with scissors. In a shorter straw the standing wave inside is shorter too, so the pitch is higher; in a longer straw the note is lower.
deep: The reed

The bevelled lips act as a reed. When you blow, there is high pressure in your mouth; as air rushes through the straw, the pressure in the straw drops; the high pressure outside pushes the sides of the reed inward, closing off the flow; the pressure then builds inside and pops the reed open again.
Resonance

The sound is an example of resonance: when you vibrate something at its natural frequency, the vibrations build and grow more and more extreme. The straw resonates when the sound waves bouncing back and forth inside make a standing wave, and the exact note depends on the length of the straw.
Newton was wrong, Laplace was right

Newton argued that heat was conducted between regions so rapidly that the temperature could not rise or fall. Feynman: “This argument gives the isothermal speed of sound, and it is wrong.” Laplace put forward the opposite idea, that the changes are adiabatic, so compression raises the temperature, and the correct result followed: the speed of sound depends only on the gas temperature and not on the pressure or the density.
Going further
Slide a slightly larger straw onto the end and use it like a trombone. Speed equals wavelength times frequency: at about 350 metres per second, a 350-hertz note has a wavelength of one metre.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, ch. 47 · Exploratorium Science Snacks: Straw Oboe, Organ Pipe

tiles.cap: A $99 e-reader 5.95 mm thin that magnets to the back of your phone. Catch: no Kindle app
tiles.nums: the weight of the Xteink X4 Pro, with a 4.3-inch, 219-ppi screen and an 1100 mAh battery
tiles.p1: TIME put the Xteink X4 Pro on its Best Inventions of 2026 list on 15 October: an e-reader small enough to pocket that can magnetically snap to the back of a smartphone, now with a touchscreen, adjustable warm-and-cool front lighting and a larger battery. Xteink’s spec page: 4.3-inch screen at 219 ppi, 1100 mAh battery, 72 g, 111 × 69 × 5.95 mm, a 16 GB microSD card in the box (expandable to 256 GB), Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth. There is no ebook storefront; its unlocked firmware means you upload your own EPUBs.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s James Rogerson, after a month, called the interface “ugly and clunky”; no Android means it can’t run the Kindle or Kobo apps, and it charges through what he calls a “slightly fiddly proprietary charger” (a pogo-pin port, per Xteink) rather than USB-C.
deep: The engineering choice

Rogerson’s guess for the proprietary charger: “presumably in an effort to keep this as small as possible”. Xteink’s own FAQ confirms a charging cable is not included in the box. The battery “seems long-lasting too”, he wrote; Xteink gives no hours figure, only 1100 mAh.
Pixels

219 pixels per inch on a 4.3-inch screen; look up the ppi of your phone and compare. The screen is a front-lit panel with adjustable brightness and warm/cool light, and page turns work by tap, swipe or physical buttons.
The magnets

Rogerson: the magnets “weren’t strong enough to securely attach it to my phone while in a case”, and it can shift around and come loose in a pocket. He still called it “a pleasure to read books on”, and “thin enough that it doesn’t stick out much beyond the camera bump” of his iPhone.
Who it is for

Formats are EPUB and TXT, with JPG and BMP images. Because many bought ebooks need their DRM removed first, and new firmware must be flashed to get the most out of it, Rogerson “can’t really recommend this to the average ebook reader”. Price: $99 on Xteink’s site, down from a listed $129, though it was showing as sold out this weekend.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026, 15 Oct 2026 (Eliza Thompson) · Xteink spec page · TechRadar, 29 Aug 2026 (James Rogerson)
